CHAPTER VII.



The Curates at Tea.





[[Caroline Helstone]] was just eighteen years old, and at eighteen the true

narrative of life is yet to be commenced. Before that [[Time|time]] we sit

listening to a tale, a marvellous fiction, delightful sometimes, and sad

sometimes, almost always unreal. Before that [[Time|time]] our world is heroic,

its inhabitants half-divine or semi-demon; its scenes are dream-scenes;

darker woods and stranger hills, brighter skies, more dangerous waters,

sweeter [[Flowers|flowers]], more tempting fruits, wider plains, drearier deserts,

sunnier fields than are found in [[Nature|nature]], overspread our enchanted globe.

What a [[Moon|moon]] we gaze on before that [[Time|time]]! How the trembling of our hearts

at her aspect bears witness to its unutterable [[Beauty|beauty]]! As to our sun, it

is a burning heaven--the world of gods.



At that [[Time|time]], at eighteen, drawing near the confines of illusive, void

[[Dreams|dreams]], Elf-land lies behind us, the shores of Reality rise in front.

These shores are yet distant; they look so blue, soft, gentle, we long

to reach them. In sunshine we see a greenness beneath the azure, as of

[[Spring|spring]] meadows; we catch glimpses of silver lines, and imagine the roll

of living waters. Could we but reach this land, we think to hunger and

thirst no more; whereas many a wilderness, and often the flood of [[Death|death]],

or some stream of sorrow as cold and almost as black as [[Death|death]], is to be

crossed ere true bliss can be tasted. Every joy that life gives must be

earned ere it is secured; and how hardly earned, those only know who

have wrestled for great prizes. The heart's [[Blood|blood]] must gem with red

beads the brow of the combatant, before the wreath of victory rustles

over it.



At eighteen we are not aware of this. [[Hope]], when she smiles on us, and

promises happiness to-morrow, is implicitly believed; [[Love]], when he

comes wandering like a lost angel to our door, is at once admitted,

welcomed, embraced. His quiver is not seen; if his arrows penetrate,

their wound is like a thrill of new life. There are no fears of [[Poison|poison]],

none of the barb which no leech's hand can extract. That perilous

passion--an agony ever in some of its phases; with many, an agony

throughout--is believed to be an unqualified good. In short, at eighteen

the school of experience is to be entered, and her humbling, crushing,

grinding, but yet purifying and invigorating lessons are yet to be

learned.



Alas, Experience! No other [[Mentor|mentor]] has so wasted and frozen a face as

yours, none wears a robe so black, none bears a rod so heavy, none with

hand so inexorable draws the novice so sternly to his task, and forces

him with authority so resistless to its acquirement. It is by your

instructions [[Alone|alone]] that man or woman can ever find a safe track through

life's wilds; without it, how they stumble, how they stray! On what

forbidden grounds do they intrude, down what dread declivities are they

hurled!



Caroline, having been convoyed [[Home|home]] by Robert, had no wish to pass what

remained of the evening with her uncle. The room in which he sat was

very sacred ground to her; she seldom intruded on it; and to-[[Night|night]] she

kept aloof till the bell rang for prayers. Part of the evening church

service was the form of worship observed in Mr. Helstone's household. He

read it in his usual nasal voice, clear, loud, and monotonous. The rite

over, his niece, according to her wont, stepped up to him.



"Good-[[Night|night]], uncle."



"Hey! You've been gadding abroad all day--visiting, dining out, and what

not!"



"Only at the cottage."



"And have you learned your lessons?"



"Yes."



"And made a shirt?"



"Only part of one."



"[[Well]], that will do. Stick to the needle, learn shirt-making and

gown-making and piecrust-making, and you'll be a clever woman some day.

Go to bed now. I'm busy with a pamphlet here."



Presently the niece was enclosed in her small bedroom, the door bolted,

her white dressing-gown assumed, her long hair loosened and falling

thick, soft, and wavy to her waist; and as, resting from the task of

combing it out, she leaned her check on her hand and fixed her eyes on

the carpet, before her [[Rose|rose]], and close around her drew, the visions we

see at eighteen years.



Her thoughts were speaking with her, speaking pleasantly, as it seemed,

for she smiled as she listened. She looked pretty meditating thus; but a

brighter thing than she was in that apartment--the spirit of youthful

[[Hope]]. According to this flattering [[Prophet|prophet]], she was to know

disappointment, to feel chill no more; she had entered on the [[Dawn|dawn]] of a

[[Summer|summer]] day--no false [[Dawn|dawn]], but the true [[Spring|spring]] of morning--and her sun

would quickly rise. Impossible for her now to suspect that she was the

sport of delusion; her expectations seemed warranted, the foundation on

which they rested appeared solid.



"When people [[Love|love]], the next step is they marry," was her argument. "Now,

I [[Love|love]] Robert, and I feel sure that Robert loves me. I have thought so

many a [[Time|time]] before; to-day I _felt_ it. When I looked up at him after

repeating Chénier's poem, his eyes (what handsome eyes he has!) sent the

[[Truth|truth]] through my heart. Sometimes I am afraid to speak to him, lest I

should be too frank, lest I should seem forward--for I have more than

once regretted bitterly overflowing, superfluous words, and feared I had

said more than he expected me to say, and that he would disapprove what

he might deem my indiscretion; now, to-[[Night|night]] I could have ventured to

express any thought, he was so indulgent. How kind he was as we walked

up the lane! He does not flatter or say foolish things; his [[Love|love]]-making

([[Friendship|friendship]], I mean; of course I don't yet account him my [[Lover|lover]], but I


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO VII.



I curati a teatro.





[[Caroline Helstone]] aveva appena diciotto anni, ed a diciotto anni si compie davvero.

La narrazione della vita non è ancora iniziata. Prima di quel [[Time|momento]], noi ci sediamo.

Ascoltare una storia… una meravigliosa finzione, a volte deliziosa, altre volte triste.

A volte, quasi sempre irreale. Prima di quel [[Time|momento]], il nostro mondo era pieno di eroi.

I suoi abitanti sono metà divini, metà demoni; i suoi luoghi sono scenari onirici.

Foreste più oscure e colline più strane, cieli più luminosi, acque più pericolose…

Fiori più dolci, frutti più deliziosi, pianure più vaste, deserti ancora più desolati.

Campi più soleggiati di quelli che si trovano nella [[Nature|>natura]] coprono il nostro incantato pianeta.

Che [[Moon|luna]] ammiriamo prima di quel [[Time|momento]]. Quanto trema il nostro cuore.

Il suo aspetto stesso testimonia della sua inesprimibile [[Beauty|bellezza]]! Per quanto riguarda il nostro sole.

È un cielo ardente, il regno degli dei.



In quel [[Time|momento]], all'età di diciotto anni, vicino ai confini di un mondo illusorio e vuoto.

Nei [[Dreams|>sogni]], la Terra degli Elfi è alle nostre spalle, mentre le rive della Realtà si ergono davanti a noi.

# Queste rive sono ancora lontane… Sembrano così azzurre, morbide, dolci… Ne sentiamo la mancanza.

Per raggiungerli. Al sole, sotto il cielo azzurro, si nota un colore verde… come se…

Prati in piena [[Spring|primavera]]; intravediamo linee d’argento e immaginiamo il loro movimento ondulato.

“Delle acque vive… Se solo potessimo raggiungere questa terra…” Pensiamo che lì non ci sarebbe più fame.

Non si ha più sete; mentre molte lande desolate, e spesso anche la furia della [[Death|morte]].

O qualche flusso di dolore, freddo e quasi nero come la [[Death|morte]], che deve essere vissuto.

“Crossed ere true bliss can be tasted: every joy that life gives must be…”

#Guadagnato prima ancora di essere realmente acquisito… E quanto a fatica venga guadagnato, solo coloro che lo sperimentano lo sanno davvero.

Hanno lottato per grandi premi. Il sangue del cuore deve brillare di rosso.

# Gocce di sudore sulla fronte del combattente, prima che il ramo della vittoria fruscii…

Finito.



A diciotto anni non ci rendiamo conto di queste cose. La [[Hope|[Speranza]], quando sorride a noi.

Le promesse di felicità per domani sono credute implicitamente; l’[[Love|Amore]], quando.

“Viene a bussare alla nostra porta come un angelo smarrito… e viene subito accettata.”

Benvenuto, accolto con affetto… La sua faretra non si vede; se le sue frecce colpiscono il bersaglio…

La loro ferita è come un segnale di nuova vita. Non c’è più paura del [[Poison|veleno]].

"Nessuna delle spine che nemmeno la mano di una sanguisuga può estrarre… Quel pericolo imminente."

Passione: un’agonia, sempre presente in alcune delle sue fasi; per molti, un’agonia continua.

Si ritiene che “in ogni caso” sia una cosa assolutamente positiva. In breve, all’età di diciotto anni…

“La scuola dell’esperienza deve essere attraversata… e il suo effetto umiliante, travolgente…”

Lezioni dure, ma al contempo purificanti e rigeneranti… sono ancora da vivere.

colto.



Ahimè, Esperienza. Nessun altro [[Mentor|mentore]] ha mai sprecato e “congelato” un volto in modo così totale.

#Il tuo… nessuno indossa un abito così nero, nessuno porta un bastone così pesante… nessuno con…

# Una mano così implacabile spinge il novizio con tale fermezza verso il suo compito, e lo costringe…

#Con autorità tale da rendere impossibile resistervi… È attraverso il tuo…

Solo queste istruzioni permettono a un uomo o a una donna di trovare una strada sicura da seguire.

“Le selvaggezze della vita: senza di esse, come inciampano, come si perdono… Su cosa?”

“Territori proibiti… in quali terribili pendii osano addentrarsi?”

Scagliato via!



Caroline, essendo stata riaccompagnata a casa da Robert, non aveva alcun desiderio di rivivere ciò che.

Trascorse il resto della serata con suo zio. La stanza in cui si trovava…

Per lei era un luogo estremamente sacro; raramente vi metteva piede; e di notte.

Tenuto a distanza fino al suono della campana per la preghiera… Parte della funzione serale in chiesa.

Nella casa del signor Helstone, il modo di venerare Dio consisteva nel prestare servizio agli altri. Lui…

Lo lesse con la sua solita voce nasale, chiara, forte e monotona… Il rituale.

Ecco che, come era sua abitudine, sua nipote si avvicinò a lui.



“Buona [[Night|notte]], zio.”



"Ehi! Sei stato via tutto il giorno: visitando, mangiando fuori e chissà cosa ancora..."

“No, davvero!”



"Solo nella capanna."



“E hai imparato la lezione?”



“Sì, davvero.”



“E ha fatto anche una camicia?”



“Solo una parte di uno.”



“Beh, va bene così. Concentrati sul cucito a maglia, impara a fare camicie, ”

Fare abiti e preparare le crostate, un giorno diventerai davvero una donna intelligente.

Vai a letto ora. Sono occupato a lavorare su un opuscolo qui.



In quel momento, la nipote si trovava chiusa nella sua piccola camera da letto, con la porta sbarrata.

# Indossata la sua vestaglia bianca, i suoi lunghi capelli sciolti e che le ricadevano sulle spalle

Lunga, morbida e ondulata fino alla vita… E mentre riposava dopo aver svolto quel compito…

# Mettendoci d’impegno, appoggiò il foglio sulle mani e fissò lo sguardo…

Il tappeto, davanti alla sua [[Rose|rosa]] e intorno a lei, evocava quelle visioni che.

Vederlo a diciotto anni.



I suoi pensieri sembravano parlare con lei, in modo piacevole…

“Perché sorrideva mentre ascoltava… Sembrava davvero assorta in profonda riflessione…”

“Qualcosa di più luminoso di lei in quell’appartamento… lo spirito della giovinezza.”

[[Hope|[Speranza]]. Secondo questo lusinghiero [[Prophet|profeta]], lei avrebbe dovuto saperlo.

Delusione, non sentire più freddo. Aveva appena iniziato l’alba di una nuova fase.

Una giornata d’estate, senza un falso alba, ma la vera primavera del mattino, e il suo sole.

Il titolo aumenterebbe rapidamente… Ora è impossibile che lei sospetti di essere quella persona.

#Gioco di illusione; le sue aspettative sembravano giustificate, la base su cui…

Quello su cui riposavano sembrava solido.



“Quando le persone si [[Love|amano]], il passo successivo è sposarsi,” era il suo ragionamento. “Ora, ”

Amo Robert, e sono sicura che anche lui mi ami. L’ho sempre pensato così.

Molte volte in passato; oggi l’ho _sentito_ davvero. Quando l’ho guardato di nuovo dopo.

#Ripetendo il poema di Chénier, i suoi occhi… che occhi bellissimi che ha!

La [[Truth|verità]] è nel mio cuore. A volte ho paura di parlargli, per non.

Titolo:  
Dovrei essere troppo franco, altrimenti sembrerei audace… poiché ho molto di più da offrire.

Titolo:  
Parole una volta amareggiamente scritte in eccesso… e di cui temevo di averne troppo detto.

Disse più di quanto si aspettasse che dicessi io, e manifestò chiaramente il suo disapprovamento…

Potrebbe considerare la mia indiscrezione. Ora, di notte, avrei potuto osare fare qualcosa.

Non esprimeva mai alcun pensiero; era davvero troppo indulgente… Quanto fosse gentile mentre camminavamo insieme.

Avanti con decisione! Non lusinga nessuno né dice sciocchezze; il suo modo di manifestare l’amore.

Intendo dire l’[[Friendship|amicizia]]; ovviamente non lo considero ancora il mio [[Lover|amante]], ma.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_07--part_02" data-title="Shirley — Chapter 7 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 07" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/bees,motif/flowers,motif/garden,motif/marriage,motif/rose,motif/spring,motif/time,motif/window,concept/hope,concept/truth,character/mermaid"></span>


[[Hope|hope]] he will be so some day) is not like what we read of in books,--it

is far better--original, quiet, manly, sincere. I _do_ like him; I would

be an excellent wife to him if he did marry me; I would tell him of his

faults (for he has a few faults), but I would study his comfort, and

cherish him, and do my best to make him happy. Now, I am sure he will

not be cold to-morrow. I feel almost certain that to-morrow evening he

will either come here, or ask me to go there."



She recommenced combing her hair, long as a [[Mermaid|mermaid]]'s. Turning her head

as she arranged it she saw her own face and form in the glass. Such

reflections are soberizing to plain people: their own eyes are not

enchanted with the image; they are confident then that the eyes of

others can see in it no fascination. But the fair must naturally draw

other conclusions: the picture is charming, and must charm. Caroline saw

a shape, a head, that, daguerreotyped in that attitude and with that

expression, would have been lovely. She could not choose but derive

from the spectacle confirmation to her hopes. It was then in

undiminished gladness she sought her couch.



And in undiminished gladness she [[Rose|rose]] the next day. As she entered her

uncle's breakfast-room, and with soft cheerfulness wished him

good-morning, even that little man of bronze himself thought, for an

instant, his niece was growing "a fine girl." Generally she was quiet

and timid with him--very docile, but not communicative; this morning,

however, she found many things to say. Slight topics [[Alone|alone]] might be

discussed between them; for with a woman--a girl--Mr. Helstone would

touch on no other. She had taken an early walk in the [[Garden|garden]], and she

told him what [[Flowers|flowers]] were beginning to [[Spring|spring]] there; she inquired when

the gardener was to come and trim the borders; she informed him that

certain starlings were beginning to build their nests in the

church-tower (Briarfield church was close to Briarfield rectory); she

wondered the tolling of [[The Bells|the bells]] in the belfry did not scare them.



Mr. Helstone opined that "they were like other fools who had just

paired--insensible to inconvenience just for the moment." Caroline, made

perhaps a little too courageous by her temporary good spirits, here

hazarded a remark of a kind she had never before ventured to make on

observations dropped by her revered relative.



"Uncle," said she, "whenever you speak of [[Marriage|marriage]] you speak of it

scornfully. Do you think people shouldn't marry?"



"It is decidedly the wisest plan to remain single, especially for

women."



"Are all marriages unhappy?"



"Millions of marriages are unhappy. If everybody confessed the [[Truth|truth]],

perhaps all are more or less so."



"You are always vexed when you are asked to come and marry a couple.

Why?"



"Because one does not like to act as accessory to the commission of a

piece of pure folly."



Mr. Helstone spoke so readily, he seemed rather glad of the opportunity

to give his niece a piece of his mind on this point. Emboldened by the

impunity which had hitherto attended her questions, she went a little

further.



"But why," said she, "should it be pure folly? If two people like each

other, why shouldn't they consent to live together?"



"They tire of each other--they tire of each other in a month. A

yokefellow is not a companion; he or she is a fellow-sufferer."



It was by no means naïve simplicity which inspired Caroline's next

remark; it was a sense of antipathy to such opinions, and of displeasure

at him who held them.



"One would think you had never been married, uncle. One would think you

were an old bachelor."



"Practically, I am so."



"But you have been married. Why were you so inconsistent as to marry?"



"Every man is mad once or twice in his life."



"So you tired of my aunt, and my aunt of you, and you were miserable

together?"



Mr. Helstone pushed out his cynical lip, wrinkled his brown forehead,

and gave an inarticulate grunt.



"Did she not suit you? Was she not good-tempered? Did you not get used

to her? Were you not sorry when she died?"



"Caroline," said Mr. Helstone, bringing his hand slowly down to within

an inch or two of the table, and then smiting it suddenly on the

mahogany, "understand this: it is vulgar and puerile to confound

generals with particulars. In every case there is the rule and there are

the exceptions. Your questions are stupid and babyish. Ring the bell, if

you have done breakfast."



The breakfast was taken away, and that meal over, it was the general

custom of uncle and niece to separate, and not to meet again till

dinner; but to-day the niece, instead of quitting the room, went to the

[[Window|window]]-seat, and sat down there. Mr. Helstone looked round uneasily once

or twice, as if he wished her away; but she was gazing from the [[Window|window]],

and did not seem to mind him: so he continued the perusal of his morning

paper--a particularly interesting one it chanced to be, as new movements

had just taken place in the Peninsula, and certain columns of the

journal were rich in long dispatches from General Lord Wellington. He

little knew, meantime, what thoughts were busy in his niece's

mind--thoughts the conversation of the past half-hour had revived but

not generated; tumultuous were they now, as disturbed [[Bees|bees]] in a hive,

but it was years since they had first made their cells in her brain.



She was reviewing his character, his disposition, repeating his

sentiments on [[Marriage|marriage]]. Many a [[Time|time]] had she reviewed them before, and

sounded the gulf between her own mind and his; and then, on the other

side of the wide and deep chasm, she had seen, and she now saw, another

figure standing beside her uncle's--a strange shape, dim, sinister,

scarcely earthly--the half-remembered image of her own father, James

Helstone, Matthewson Helstone's brother.

La [[Hope|>speranza]] che un giorno possa essere così non è come quella che leggiamo nei libri, –non è affatto la stessa.

“Molto meglio… originale, tranquillo, virile, sincero. Mi piace davvero; lo sceglierei senza esitazione.”

#Sarei una moglie eccellente per lui se mi sposasse; gli racconterei di…

“Ha alcuni difetti, ma osserverei con attenzione il suo modo di vivere comodamente…”

“Custodiscilo con affetto e fai del tuo meglio per renderlo felice… Ora sono sicura che lo sarà.”

“Non farà freddo domani… Sono quasi certo che stasera…”

O verrà qui, o mi chiederà di andare lì.



Riprese a pettinarsi i capelli, lunghi come quelli di una [[Mermaid|>sirena]], e girò la testa.

#Nella superficie del vetro, vide il proprio volto e la propria figura riflessi.

“Le riflessioni sono un monito per le persone comuni: i loro stessi occhi non mentono.”

Titolo:  
Incantati dall’immagine; allora sono certi che i loro occhi…

Altri non vi vedono alcuna fascinazione… Ma una bella donna, naturalmente, attira l’attenzione.

Altre conclusioni: il dipinto è incantevole, e di certo deve incantare… Caroline lo vide così.

# Una forma, una testa… immortalate nella posizione e con quell’aspetto…

# Un’espressione che sarebbe stata incantevole… Non le restò altra scelta se non quella di lasciarsi guidare da essa.

Dalla conferma di quella visione alle sue speranze… Fu allora che…

Con una gioia inesauribile, andò a sdraiarsi sul suo divano.



E con la stessa gioia inesauribile, il giorno dopo si alzò. Mentre entrava nella sua.

# La sala da pranzo dello zio, e con una dolce allegria gli augurò…

Buongiorno… anche quel piccolo uomo di bronzo lo pensò, infatti.

In un attimo, sua nipote stava diventando “una bella ragazza”. Di solito era silenziosa.

E timida con lui… molto docile, ma non comunicativa; stamattina…

Tuttavia, aveva molte cose da dire. Anche argomenti semplici e banali potevano essere.

Fu argomentato tra loro; perché con una donna… una ragazza… il signor Helstone avrebbe…

Non affrontò altri argomenti. Aveva fatto una passeggiata mattutina nel [[Garden|giardino]] e poi.

Gli raccontò quali [[Flowers|>fiori]] stavano iniziando a sbocciare lì; chiese quando.

Il giardiniere sarebbe venuto a potare i bordi del prato; glielo aveva detto lei stessa.

#Alcuni sterne iniziavano già a costruire i loro nidi

#Chiesa-torre (La chiesa di Briarfield era vicina alla residenza parrocchiale di Briarfield)

Si chiedeva come mai il suono delle campane nella torre campanaria non li spaventasse.



“Secondo il signor Helstone, erano come tutti gli altri sciocchi che…”

#"Paarati – insensibili alle scomodità, almeno per il momento…“ Caroline, disse."

“Forse un po’ troppo coraggiosa, data la sua temporanea buona disposizione…”

Osò fare un commento del genere che non aveva mai osato fare prima.

Le osservazioni fatte dal suo rispettato parente furono ignorate.



“Zio,” disse lei, “ogni volta che parli di [[Marriage|mattrimono]], lo fai sempre in quel modo, ”

Con disprezzo. Pensi che le persone non dovrebbero sposarsi?



#Rimanere single è decisamente il piano più saggio, soprattutto per…

donne.”



“Tutti i matrimoni sono infelici?”



“Milioni di matrimoni sono infelici. Se tutti confessassero la [[Truth|verità]],”

Forse tutti sono più o meno così.



“Sei sempre infastidito quando ti chiedono di venire a sposare qualcuno.”

“Perché?”



#"Perché a nessuno piace essere complice nell’attuazione di un atto del genere..."

“Un vero e proprio atto di follia pura.”



# Mr. Helstone parlava con tale disinvoltura che sembrava davvero felice di quell’opportunità

#Per fargli capire chiaramente la sua posizione su questa questione… Incoraggiato dal fatto che…

“L’impunità che fino ad allora aveva accompagnato le sue domande… la spinse a procedere oltre.”

inoltre.



“Ma perché,” disse lei, “dovrebbe essere una pura follia? Se due persone si piacciono a vicenda…”

Inoltre, perché non dovrebbero essere d’accordo ad vivere insieme?



“Si stancano l’uno dell’altro… si stancano già dopo un mese.”

Un compagno di catena non è un vero amico; lui o lei è semplicemente una persona che soffre insieme a te.



#Non era affatto una semplicità ingenua quella che ispirò il prossimo passo di Caroline

# Un senso di avversione verso tali opinioni, e di disappunto…

verso colui che le teneva in mano.



“Si direbbe che non siate mai stati sposati, zio… Si direbbe…”

Era un vecchio scapolo.



“Praticamente, è proprio così.”



“Ma sei stato sposato. Perché sei stato così incoerente da sposarti?”



Ogni uomo impazzisce una o due volte nella sua vita.



#"Vi siete stancati sia di mia zia che di me, e quindi eravate infelici..."

“Insieme?”



# Mr. Helstone contrasse le labbra in un’espressione cinica e corrugò la fronte marrone.

E emise un grugnito inarticolato.



#"Non ti piaceva? Non era di buon carattere? Non ti sei abituato..."

A lei? Non ti è dispiaciuto quando è morta?”



“Caroline,” disse il signor Helstone, abbassando lentamente la mano verso di lei…

“Un pollice o due di distanza dal tavolo… e poi colpirlo improvvisamente…”

Titolo:  
“Mahogany… Capite bene questo: è volgare e infantile confondere…”

Generali con particolari: in ogni caso esistono le regole…

Le eccezioni… Le tue domande sono stupide e infantili. Ti suona qualcosa?

Hai preparato la colazione.



Il breakfast fu portato via, e una volta terminata quella colazione, arrivò il momento…

Titolo:  
L’usanza del zio e della nipote di separarsi e di non rivedersi mai più…

Cena… ma oggi la nipote, invece di lasciare la stanza, è andata…

Un posto vicino alla [[Window|finestra]], e si sedette lì. Il signor Helstone guardò intorno con inquietudine una volta.

O due volte, come se volesse farla scomparire. Ma lei continuava a guardare fuori dalla [[Window|finestra]].

#E non sembrava che gli desse fastidio; quindi continuò a leggere il suo giornale mattutino.

Titolo:  
Un articolo particolarmente interessante… proprio quello che ci serviva per comprendere i nuovi movimenti in corso.

# Aveva appena avuto luogo nella penisola, e alcune colonne…

Il giornale era ricco di lunghi resoconti inviati dal generale Lord Wellington.

Poche persone sapevano, intanto, quali pensieri agitassero la mente di sua nipote…

Titolo:  
I pensieri… La conversazione degli ultimi trenta minuti li avevano rinvigoriti, ma…

Non è stato generato alcun testo; ora erano nel caos, come api disturbate in un alveare.

Ma erano passati molti anni da quando avevano creato per la prima volta quelle cellule nel suo cervello.



# Stava valutando il suo carattere, il suo temperamento, ripetendo le sue…

Sentimenti sul [[Marriage|matrimonio]]. Molte volte in passato li aveva riletti.

# Rivelava il divario tra i suoi pensieri e quelli di lui…

Sul lato di quell’abisso ampio e profondo, lei aveva visto… e ora vedeva ancora qualcos’altro.

#"Figura che sta accanto a suo zio: una forma strana, sfocata, inquietante..."

Appena terrena… quell’immagine appena ricordata di suo padre, James.

Helstone, il fratello di Matthewson Helstone.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_07--part_03" data-title="Shirley — Chapter 7 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 07" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/lover,motif/clock,motif/cross,motif/garden,motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/road,motif/silence,motif/time,concept/doubt,concept/nature,concept/self,character/phantom"></span>


Rumours had reached her ear of what that father's character was; old

servants had dropped hints; she knew, too, that he was not a good man,

and that he was never kind to her. She recollected--a dark recollection

it was--some weeks that she had spent with him in a great town

somewhere, when she had had no maid to dress her or take care of her;

when she had been shut up, day and [[Night|night]], in a high garret-room, without

a carpet, with a bare uncurtained bed, and scarcely any other furniture;

when he went out early every morning, and often forgot to return and

give her her dinner during the day, and at [[Night|night]], when he came back, was

like a madman, furious, terrible, or--still more painful--like an idiot,

imbecile, senseless. She knew she had fallen ill in this place, and that

one [[Night|night]], when she was very sick he had come raving into the room, and

said he would kill her, for she was a burden to him. Her screams had

brought aid; and from the moment she was then rescued from him she had

never seen him, except as a dead man in his coffin.



That was her father. Also she had a mother, though Mr. Helstone never

spoke to her of that mother, though she could not remember having seen

her; but that she was alive she knew. This mother was then the

drunkard's wife. What had _their_ [[Marriage|marriage]] been? Caroline, turning from

the lattice, whence she had been watching the starlings (though without

seeing them), in a low voice, and with a sad, bitter tone, thus broke

the [[Silence|silence]] of the room,--



"You term [[Marriage|marriage]] miserable, I suppose, from what you saw of my father

and mother's. If my mother suffered what I suffered when I was with

papa, she must have had a dreadful life."



Mr. Helstone, thus addressed, wheeled about in his chair, and looked

over his spectacles at his niece. He was taken aback.



Her father and mother! What had put it into her head to mention her

father and mother, of whom he had never, during the twelve years she had

lived with him, spoken to her? That the thoughts were [[Self|self]]-matured, that

she had any recollections or speculations about her parents, he could

not fancy.



"Your father and mother? Who has been talking to you about them?"



"Nobody; but I remember something of what papa was, and I pity mamma.

Where is she?"



This "Where is she?" had been on Caroline's lips hundreds of times

before, but till now she had never uttered it.



"I hardly know," returned Mr. Helstone; "I was little acquainted with

her. I have not heard from her for years: but wherever she is, she

thinks nothing of you; she never inquires about you. I have reason to

believe she does not wish to see you. Come, it is school-[[Time|time]]. You go to

your cousin at ten, don't you? The [[Clock|clock]] has struck."



Perhaps Caroline would have said more; but Fanny, coming in, informed

her master that the churchwardens wanted to speak to him in the vestry.

He hastened to join them, and his niece presently set out for the

cottage.



The [[Road|road]] from the rectory to Hollow's Mill inclined downwards; she ran,

therefore, almost all the way. Exercise, the fresh air, the thought of

seeing Robert, at least of being on his premises, in his vicinage,

revived her somewhat depressed spirits quickly. Arriving in sight of the

white [[house]], and within hearing of the thundering mill and its rushing

watercourse, the first thing she saw was Moore at his [[Garden|garden]] gate. There

he stood, in his belted Holland blouse, a light cap covering his head,

which undress costume suited him. He was looking down the lane, not in

the direction of his cousin's approach. She stopped, withdrawing a

little behind a willow, and studied his appearance.



"He has not his peer," she thought. "He is as handsome as he is

intelligent. What a keen eye he has! What clearly-cut, spirited

features--thin and serious, but graceful! I do like his face, I do like

his aspect, I do like him so much--better than any of those shuffling

curates, for instance--better than anybody; bonny Robert!"



She sought "bonny Robert's" presence speedily. For his part, when she

challenged his sight, I believe he would have passed from before her

eyes like a [[Phantom|phantom]], if he could; but being a tall fact, and no fiction,

he was obliged to stand the greeting. He made it brief. It was

cousin-like, brother-like, friend-like, anything but [[Lover|lover]]-like. The

nameless charm of last [[Night|night]] had left his manner: he was no longer the

same man: or, at any rate, the same heart did not beat in his breast.

Rude disappointment, sharp [[Cross|cross]]! At first the eager girl would not

believe in the change, though she saw and felt it. It was difficult to

withdraw her hand from his, till he had bestowed at least something like

a kind pressure; it was difficult to turn her eyes from his eyes, till

his looks had expressed something more and fonder than that cool

welcome.



A [[Lover|lover]] masculine so disappointed can speak and urge explanation, a

[[Lover|lover]] feminine can say nothing; if she did, the result would be shame

and anguish, inward remorse for [[Self|self]]-treachery. [[Nature]] would brand such

demonstration as a rebellion against her instincts, and would

vindictively repay it afterwards by the thunderbolt of [[Self|self]]-contempt

smiting suddenly in secret. Take the matter as you find it: ask no

questions, utter no remonstrances; it is your best wisdom. You expected

bread, and you have got a stone: break your teeth on it, and don't

shriek because the nerves are martyrized; do not [[Doubt|doubt]] that your mental

stomach--if you have such a thing--is strong as an ostrich's; the stone

will digest. You held out your hand for an egg, and fate put into it a

scorpion. Show no consternation: close your fingers firmly upon the

gift; let it sting through your palm. Never mind; in [[Time|time]], after your

hand and arm have swelled and quivered long with torture, the squeezed


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Aveva sentito voci riguardo al carattere di quel padre… vecchie voci.

I servitori avevano fatto dei sottintesi; anche lei sapeva che non era un uomo buono.

# E che non fu mai gentile con lei. Lei se ne ricordava… un ricordo cupo.

# Erano trascorse alcune settimane da quando aveva trascorso del tempo con lui in una grande città

Da qualche parte, quando non aveva più una cameriera che la vestisse o si prendesse cura di lei…

Quando era stata rinchiusa, giorno e [[Night|notte]], in una soffitta alta, senza.

Un tappeto, un letto scoperto e senza tende, e quasi nessun altro mobile…

#Quando usciva presto ogni mattina, e spesso dimenticava di tornare…

Le dava la cena durante il giorno, e di [[Night|notte]], quando tornava a casa, faceva.

Come un pazzo furioso, terribile… o, ancora peggio, come un idiota.

Imbecile, insensato… Sapeva di essere ammalata in questo posto, e che…

Una [[Night|notte]], quando lei era molto malata, lui entrò nella stanza delirando.

Disse che l’avrebbe uccisa, perché era un peso per lui… I suoi urla…

Portò aiuto; e dal momento in cui fu salvata da lui, lei…

Non l’avevo mai visto, se non come un uomo morto nella sua bara.



#Quello era suo padre… Ma aveva anche una madre, sebbene il signor Helstone non ne parlasse mai.

Le parlò di quella madre, anche se lei non ricordava di averla mai vista.

# Lei… ma sapeva che era viva. Allora, questa madre era…

La moglie di un ubriacone. Che tipo di [[Marriage|matrimonio]] avevano avuto? Caroline, voltandosi.

Il reticolo da cui aveva osservato gli storni… (sebbene senza…)

(vedendoli), a bassa voce e con un tono triste e amaro, disse così

Il [[Silence|silenzio]] della stanza.



“Defini il [[Marriage|matrimonio]] una cosa miserabile, suppongo, a giudicare da ciò che hai visto di mio padre, ”

#Della madre e mio… Se mia madre avesse sofferto ciò che ho sofferto io quando ero con lei…

“Papà, deve aver vissuto una vita terribile.”



# Mr. Helstone, così chiamato, girò sulla sedia e guardò…

Sotto i suoi occhiali, fissava sua nipote. Rimase sbalordito.



“Il suo padre e sua madre… Che le era venuto in mente di menzionarli?”

“Padre e madre… di cui non aveva mai saputo nulla, nei dodici anni in cui lei era stata…”

Gli è vissuta accanto, le ha parlato? Che quei pensieri si siano formati da soli, che.

# Quali ricordi o congetture avesse riguardo ai suoi genitori…

Niente di sofisticato.



“Tuo padre e tua madre? Chi ti ha parlato di loro?”



“Nessuno. Ma ricordo qualcosa di ciò che papà era, e provo compassione per mamma.”

“Dove è?”



“Dove è?” Questa domanda era stata ripetuta centinaia di volte dalle labbra di Caroline.

Prima d’ora, ma fino ad ora non l’aveva mai pronunciato.



“Non ne so molto,” rispose il signor Helstone; “non conoscevo bene quella persona.”

“Lei… Non ho più avuto sue notizie da anni; ma ovunque si trovi, lei…”

Non pensa affatto a te; non si informa mai su di te. Ho motivo di…

Credo che lei non voglia vederti. Vieni, è ora di andare a scuola.

Tuo cugino ha dieci anni, vero? L’[[Clock|orologio]] ha appena suonato.



Forse Caroline avrebbe detto di più; ma Fanny, entrando, comunicò…

Il suo padrone, i sagrestani volevano parlargli nella sacristia.

#Si affrettò ad unirsi a loro, e presto sua nipote partì per…

Casetta di campagna.



La [[Road|strada]] che andava dalla canonica a Hollow’s Mill era in pendenza verso il basso; lei corse.

# Quindi, per quasi tutto il cammino… Esercizio fisico, aria fresca, e il pensiero…

Vedere Robert, almeno essere nei suoi dintorni, nella sua zona residenziale…

#Ripristinò rapidamente il suo umore un po’ depresso. Appena lo vide…

Una casa bianca, e al suono assordante del mulino che rimbomba e del suo vortice incessante.

Presso il corso d’acqua, la prima cosa che vide fu Moore alla porta del suo [[Garden|giardino]]. Lì.

# In piedi, con la sua camicia olandese e un berretto leggero in testa…

Il costume che gli si addiceva… Stava guardando giù per la strada, senza fissare nulla in particolare.

#La direzione dell’avvicinamento di suo cugino… Si fermò, tirandosi indietro.

Poco dietro un salice, lo osservò attentamente.



“Non ha eguali“, pensò. “È davvero bellissimo“.

# Astuto… Che occhio acuto ha! Che analisi chiara e incisiva…

# Aspetto snello e serio, ma allo stesso tempo elegante… Mi piace davvero il suo viso.

#Il suo aspetto… Mi piace davvero molto; è migliore di qualsiasi altro di quei individui incerti e indecisi.

Curate, per esempio, meglio di chiunque altro; bravo Robert!



Cercò rapidamente la presenza di “bel Robert”. Per quanto lo riguardava, lui…

“Se la sua vista fosse stata meno debole, credo che sarebbe riuscito ad attraversare davanti a lei.”

Occhi come quelli di un [[Phantom|fantasma]], se solo potesse. Ma poiché si tratta di una realtà, non di una finzione.

# Fu costretto ad accettare quel saluto. Lo rispose brevemente.

Come un cugino, come un fratello, come un amico, ma assolutamente non come un [[Lover|innamorato]].

Il fascino senza nome di quella[[Night|notte]] aveva cambiato il suo comportamento: non era più lo stesso di prima.

Lo stesso uomo, o, comunque, non era più lo stesso cuore a battere nel suo petto.

Delusione crudele, amara [[Cross|rabbia]]. All’inizio, la ragazza ansiosa non voleva affatto.

Credere nel cambiamento, anche se lo si vedeva e lo si sentiva… Era difficile.

#Togliere la sua mano dalla sua, finché lui non avesse dato almeno qualcosa di simile...

Una sorta di pressione… Era difficile distogliere lo sguardo dai suoi occhi.

“Il suo aspetto esprimeva qualcosa di più profondo e sincero di quella freddezza apparente…”

Benvenuti.



Un [[Lover|amante]] maschile profondamente deluso può chiedere spiegazioni e insistere affinché vengano fornite.

Una donna innamorata non può dire nulla; se lo facesse, il risultato sarebbe la vergogna.

E angoscia, rimorso interiore per la tradimento verso se stessi. La [[Nature|[Natura]]] marchierebbe certamente qualcosa del genere.

"Una dimostrazione come ribellione contro i propri istinti..."

Poi lo si ripaga con vendetta, attraverso il fulmine dell’[[Self|odio di sé stesso]].

# Colpo improvviso e segreto… Accetta le cose così come sono: non chiedere nulla.

Domande… Non sollevare alcuna obiezione: è la tua massima saggezza. Te lo aspettavi.

#Pane… e invece ottieni una pietra: rompiti i denti su di essa, e non…

Grida, perché i nervi vengono messi a dura prova. Non [[Doubt|>dubitare]] mai che la tua mente.

Il ventre – se mai ne si possiede uno – è forte quanto quello di un struzzo; la pietra…

“Lo digerirò… Hai teso la mano per prendere un uovo, e il destino vi ha messo dentro qualcos’altro.”

Titolo:  
“Scorpione… Non mostrare panico: stringi forte le dita attorno…”

Un dono. Lascia che ti punga attraverso la palma della mano. Non importa; col tempo, dopo.

# Mano e braccio sono gonfi e tremanti per il lungo tormento…

scorpion will die, and you will have learned the great lesson how to

endure without a sob. For the whole remnant of your life, if you survive

the test--some, it is said, die under it--you will be stronger, wiser,

dissimulation often wearing an easy and gay mien at first, settling down

to sorrow and paleness in [[Time|time]], then passing away, and leaving a

convenient stoicism, not the less fortifying because it is half-bitter.



Half-bitter! Is that wrong? No; it should be bitter: bitterness is

strength--it is a tonic. Sweet, mild force following acute [[Suffering|suffering]] you

find nowhere; to talk of it is delusion. There may be apathetic

exhaustion after the rack. If energy remains, it will be rather a

dangerous energy--deadly when confronted with injustice.



Who has read the ballad of "Puir Mary Lee"--that old Scotch ballad,

written I know not in what generation nor by what hand? Mary had been

ill-used--probably in being made to believe that [[Truth|truth]] which was

falsehood. She is not complaining, but she is sitting [[Alone|alone]] in the

snowstorm, and you hear her thoughts. They are not the thoughts of a

model heroine under her circumstances, but they are those of a

deeply-feeling, strongly-resentful peasant-girl. Anguish has driven her

from the ingle-nook of [[Home|home]] to the white-shrouded and icy hills.

Crouched under the "cauld drift," she recalls every image of

horror--"the yellow-wymed ask," "the hairy adder," "the auld [[Moon|moon]]-bowing

tyke," "the ghaist at e'en,", "the sour bullister," "the milk on the

taed's back." She hates these, but "waur she hates Robin-a-Ree."



"Oh, ance I lived happily by yon bonny burn--

The warld was in [[Love|love]] wi' me;

But now I maun sit 'neath the cauld drift and mourn,

And curse black Robin-a-Ree!



"Then whudder awa, thou bitter biting blast,

And sough through the scrunty tree,

And smoor me up in the snaw fu' fast,

And n'er let the sun me see!



"Oh, never melt awa, thou wreath o' snaw,

That's sae kind in graving me;

But hide me frae the scorn and guffaw

O' villains like Robin-a-Ree!"



But what has been said in the last page or two is not germane to

[[Caroline Helstone]]'s feelings, or to the state of things between her and

[[Robert Moore]]. Robert had done her no wrong; he had told her no lie; it

was she that was to blame, if any one was. What bitterness her mind

distilled should and would be poured on her own head. She had loved

without being asked to [[Love|love]]--a natural, sometimes an inevitable chance,

but big with misery.



Robert, indeed, had sometimes seemed to be fond of her; but why? Because

she had made herself so pleasing to him, he could not, in spite of all

his efforts, help testifying a state of feeling his judgment did not

approve nor his will sanction. He was about to withdraw decidedly from

intimate communication with her, because he did not choose to have his

affections inextricably entangled, nor to be drawn, despite his reason,

into a [[Marriage|marriage]] he believed imprudent. Now, what was she to do? To give

way to her feelings, or to vanquish them? To pursue him, or to turn

upon herself? If she is weak, she will try the first expedient--will

lose his esteem and win his aversion; if she has sense, she will be her

own governor, and resolve to subdue and bring under guidance the

disturbed realm of her emotions. She will determine to look on life

steadily, as it is; to begin to learn its severe truths seriously, and

to study its knotty problems closely, conscientiously.



It appeared she had a little sense, for she quitted Robert quietly,

without complaint or question, without the alteration of a muscle or the

shedding of a tear, betook herself to her studies under Hortense as

usual, and at dinner-[[Time|time]] went [[Home|home]] without lingering.



When she had dined, and found herself in the rectory drawing-room [[Alone|alone]],

having left her uncle over his temperate glass of port wine, the

difficulty that occurred to and embarrassed her was, "How am I to get

through this day?"



Last [[Night|night]] she had hoped it would be spent as yesterday was, that the

evening would be again passed with happiness and Robert. She had learned

her mistake this morning; and yet she could not settle down, convinced

that no chance would occur to recall her to Hollow's Cottage, or to

bring Moore again into her society.



He had walked up after tea more than once to pass an hour with her

uncle. The door-bell had rung, his voice had been heard in the passage

just at twilight, when she little expected such a pleasure; and this had

happened twice after he had treated her with peculiar reserve; and

though he rarely talked to her in her uncle's presence, he had looked at

her relentingly as he sat opposite her work-table during his stay. The

few words he had spoken to her were comforting; his manner on bidding

her good-[[Night|night]] was genial. Now, he might come this evening, said False

[[Hope]]. She almost knew it was False [[Hope]] which breathed the whisper, and

yet she listened.



She tried to read--her thoughts wandered; she tried to sew--every stitch

she put in was an _ennui_, the occupation was insufferably tedious; she

opened her desk and attempted to write a French composition--she wrote

nothing but mistakes.



Suddenly the door-bell sharply rang; her heart leaped; she sprang to the

drawing-room door, opened it softly, peeped through the aperture. Fanny

was admitting a visitor--a gentleman--a tall man--just the height of

Robert. For one second she thought it was Robert--for one second she

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_07--part_05" data-title="Shirley — Chapter 7 (part 5)" data-chapter="Chapter 07" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/night,motif/road,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/fear,concept/truth,form/novel,histref/bible,character/chorus,character/speed,character/sunday"></span>


exulted; but the voice asking for Mr. Helstone undeceived her. That

voice was an Irish voice, consequently not Moore's, but the

curate's--Malone's. He was ushered into the dining-room, where,

doubtless, he speedily helped his rector to empty the decanters.



It was a fact to be noted, that at whatever [[house]] in Briarfield,

Whinbury, or Nunnely one curate dropped in to a meal--dinner or tea, as,

the case might be--another presently followed, often two more. Not that

they gave each other the rendezvous, but they were usually all on the

run at the same [[Time|time]]; and when Donne, for instance, sought Malone at his

lodgings and found him not, he inquired whither he had posted, and

having learned of the landlady his destination, hastened with all [[Speed|speed]]

after him. The same causes operated in the same way with Sweeting. Thus

it chanced on that afternoon that Caroline's ears were three times

tortured with the ringing of the bell and the advent of undesired

guests; for Donne followed Malone, and Sweeting followed Donne; and more

wine was ordered up from the cellar into the dining-room (for though old

Helstone chid the inferior priesthood when he found them "carousing," as

he called it, in their own tents, yet at his hierarchical table he ever

liked to treat them to a glass of his best), and through the closed

doors Caroline heard their boyish laughter, and the vacant cackle of

their voices. Her [[Fear|fear]] was lest they should stay to tea, for she had no

pleasure in making tea for that particular trio. What distinctions

people draw! These three were men--young men--educated men, like Moore;

yet, for her, how great the difference! Their society was a bore--his a

delight.



Not only was she destined to be favoured with their clerical company,

but Fortune was at this moment bringing her four other guests--lady

guests, all packed in a pony-phaeton now [[rolling]] somewhat heavily along

the [[Road|road]] from Whinbury: an elderly lady and three of her buxom daughters

were coming to see her "in a friendly way," as the custom of that

neighbourhood was. Yes, a fourth [[Time|time]] the bell clanged. Fanny brought

the present announcement to the drawing-room,--



"Mrs. Sykes and the three Misses Sykes."



When Caroline was going to receive company, her habit was to wring her

hands very nervously, to flush a little, and come forward hurriedly yet

hesitatingly, wishing herself meantime at Jericho. She was, at such

crises, sadly deficient in finished manner, though she had once been at

school a year. Accordingly, on this occasion, her small white hands

sadly maltreated each other, while she stood up, waiting the entrance of

Mrs. Sykes.



In stalked that lady, a tall, bilious gentlewoman, who made an ample and

not altogether insincere profession of piety, and was greatly given to

hospitality towards the clergy. In sailed her three daughters, a showy

trio, being all three [[Well|well]]-grown, and more or less handsome.



In English country ladies there is this point to be remarked. Whether

young or old, pretty or plain, dull or sprightly, they all (or almost

all) have a certain expression stamped on their features, which seems to

say, "I know--I do not boast of it, but I _know_ that I am the standard

of what is proper; let every one therefore whom I approach, or who

approaches me, keep a sharp lookout, for wherein they differ from me--be

the same in dress, manner, opinion, principle, or practice--therein they

are wrong."



Mrs. and Misses Sykes, far from being exceptions to this observation,

were pointed illustrations of its [[Truth|truth]]. Miss Mary--a [[Well|well]]-looked,

[[Well|well]]-meant, and, on the whole, [[Well|well]]-dispositioned girl--wore her

complacency with some state, though without harshness. Miss Harriet--a

[[Beauty|beauty]]--carried it more overbearingly; she looked high and cold. Miss

Hannah, who was conceited, dashing, pushing, flourished hers consciously

and openly. The mother evinced it with the gravity proper to her age and

religious fame.



The reception was got through somehow. Caroline "was glad to see them"

(an unmitigated fib), hoped they were [[Well|well]], hoped Mrs. Sykes's cough was

better (Mrs. Sykes had had a cough for the last twenty years), hoped the

Misses Sykes had left their sisters at [[Home|home]] [[Well|well]]; to which inquiry the

Misses Sykes, sitting on three chairs opposite the music-stool, whereon

Caroline had undesignedly come to anchor, after wavering for some

seconds between it and a large arm-chair, into which she at length

recollected she ought to induct Mrs. Sykes--and indeed that lady saved

her the trouble by depositing herself therein--the Misses Sykes replied

to Caroline by one simultaneous bow, very majestic and mighty awful. A

pause followed. This bow was of a character to ensure [[Silence|silence]] for the

next five minutes, and it did. Mrs. Sykes then inquired after Mr.

Helstone, and whether he had had any return of rheumatism, and whether

preaching twice on a [[Sunday]] fatigued him, and if he was capable of

taking a full service now; and on being assured he was, she and all her

daughters, combining in [[Chorus|chorus]], expressed their opinion that he was "a

wonderful man of his years."



Pause second.



Miss Mary, getting up the steam in her turn, asked whether Caroline had

attended the [[Bible]] Society meeting which had been held at Nunnely last

[[thursday|Thursday]] [[Night|night]]. The negative answer which [[Truth|truth]] compelled Caroline to

utter--for last [[thursday|Thursday]] evening she had been sitting at [[Home|home]], reading a

[[Novel|novel]] which Robert had lent her--elicited a simultaneous expression of

surprise from the lips of the four ladies.



"We were all there," said Miss Mary--"mamma and all of us. We even

persuaded papa to go. Hannah would insist upon it. But he fell asleep

while Mr. Langweilig, the German Moravian minister, was speaking. I felt

Non solo era destinata ad godere della loro compagnia e delle loro conversazioni…

Gli ospiti, tutti ammassati in un piccolo phaeton, ora procedevano con un po’ di difficoltà.

La [[Road|strada]] che va da Whinbury: una signora anziana e tre delle sue figlie formose.

Titolo:  
Venivano a trovarla “in modo amichevole”, secondo le usanze di quel tempo.

Il quartiere era. Sì, per la quarta [[Time|volta]] il campanello suonò. Fanny portò.

# Annuncio ufficiale nella sala da pranzo…



“La signora Sykes e le tre signorine Sykes.”



# Quando Caroline aspettava visite, aveva l’abitudine di strizzare…

#Mani che tremano molto, con il viso un po’ arrossito… e si avvicinano in fretta.

Con esitazione, desiderando intanto di essere a Gerico… Lei era, in quel momento, proprio così.

Crisi… purtroppo mancante di una conclusione definitiva, anche se un tempo ne aveva avuta una.

“Scuola per un anno… Pertanto, in questa occasione, le sue piccole mani bianche…”

# Si maltrattavano a vicenda con tristezza, mentre lei si alzava in attesa dell’arrivo…

Signora Sykes.



# Inseguita da quella signora… una donna alta, dal carattere aspro, ma gentile… che suscitava molte reazioni…

# Una professione di devozione non del tutto sincera… e una grande passione per…

#Ospitalità verso il clero. Portò con sé le sue tre figlie in un viaggio sfarzoso

I tre, essendo tutti e tre ben cresciuti e più o meno attraenti, formavano un trio piuttosto interessante.



#Nel paese inglese, sulle signore c’è un aspetto da notare… Che sia o meno…

giovani o anziani, belli o semplici, noiosi o vivaci… tutti loro (o quasi)

Tutti hanno un certo espressione stampata sul loro volto, che sembra…

Titolo:  
"Dico solo che lo so… Non mi vanto di questo, ma so davvero di essere lo standard."

# Di ciò che è giusto; pertanto, chiunque mi si avvicini o…

Avvicinati a me con cautela, e osserva attentamente in cosa si distinguono da me…

Identici nel modo di vestire, nei comportamenti, nelle opinioni, nei principi e nelle azioni… In questi aspetti, sono uguali.

“Hanno torto.”



Signora e signorine Sykes: lontane dall’essere eccezioni a questa osservazione…

Erano illustrazioni concrete della sua [[Truth|verità]]. La signorina Mary – una donna di bell’aspetto.

Una ragazza di buone intenzioni, e nel complesso di ottimo carattere, indossava sempre.

“Compiacimento verso uno stato di cose, anche se senza asprezza… La signorina Harriet…”

La [[Beauty|bellezza]] la esprimeva in modo ancora più imponente; sembrava distaccata e fredda. La signorina.

Hannah, che era presuntuosa, audace e aggressiva, sfoggiava apertamente queste sue caratteristiche.

# E in modo aperto. La madre lo dimostrò con la serietà propria della sua età.

Fama religiosa.



La ricezione è riuscita comunque a svolgersi. Caroline “è stata felice di vederli”.

(una bugia senza mezzi termini, ), speravo che stessero bene, speravo che la tosse della signora Sykes fosse.

“Meglio…”, pensò la signora Sykes, che da vent’anni soffriva di tosse.

Le signorine Sykes avevano lasciato le loro sorelle a [[Home|>casa]], dove stavano bene; alla domanda su questo.

# Misses Sykes, sedute su tre sedie di fronte al pianoforte…

# Caroline aveva finito per “ancorarsi”, dopo aver esitato per un po’…

“Secondi… tra lei e un grande divano su cui alla fine si sedette.”

Ricordò che avrebbe dovuto nominare la signora Sykes membro del comitato… e infatti, quella signora aveva davvero salvato la situazione.

“Ecco il problema: si è messa proprio lì dentro…”, risposero le signorine Sykes.

“Con un unico inchino simultaneo, molto maestoso e terribilmente imponente… a Caroline.”

Seguirono delle pause. Questo inchino aveva lo scopo di garantire il [[Silence|silenzio]].

Nelle cinque minuti successivi, accadde davvero. La signora Sykes chiese poi notizie del signor.

# Helstone… e se avesse riavuto sintomi di reumatismo…

Predicare due volte in un [[Sunday|domenica]] lo stancava molto; se solo fosse stato in grado.

# Ricevendo un servizio completo ora… e una volta certa che fosse così, lei e tutti gli altri…

Le figlie, unite nel loro [[Chorus|coro]], espressero il loro parere secondo cui lui era “un, ”

Un uomo meraviglioso per la sua età.



Pausa di due secondi.



Titolo:  
Miss Mary, prendendo la sua volta, chiese se Caroline avesse…

Ha partecipato alla riunione della [[Bible|Società Biblica]] che si era tenuta a Nunnely la scorsa.

[[thursday|Giovedì]] [[Night|sera]]. Quella risposta negativa che la [[Truth|.verità]] costrinse Caroline a dare.

Assolutamente. L’ultima sera di [[thursday|>Giovedì]], lei era seduta a [[Home|>casa]], a leggere.

Il [[Novel|romanzo]] che Robert le aveva prestato suscitò in lei un'espressione di.

Una sorpresa dalle labbra delle quattro signore.



“Eravamo tutte lì,” disse la signorina Mary – “mamma e tutte noi. Anzi…”

“Persuadendo papà ad andare… Hannah insisteva, ma lui finì per addormentarsi.”

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_07--part_06" data-title="Shirley — Chapter 7 (part 6)" data-chapter="Chapter 07" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/fool,archetype/monster,motif/cross,motif/home,motif/time,concept/conversion,concept/hope,concept/regeneration,concept/self,character/phantom"></span>


quite ashamed, he nodded so."



"And there was Dr. Broadbent," cried Hannah--"such a beautiful speaker!

You couldn't expect it of him, for he is almost a vulgar-looking man."



"But such a dear man," interrupted Mary.



"And such a good man, such a useful man," added her mother.



"Only like a butcher in appearance," interposed the fair, proud Harriet.

"I couldn't bear to look at him. I listened with my eyes shut."



Miss Helstone felt her ignorance and incompetency. Not having seen Dr.

Broadbent, she could not give her opinion. Pause third came on. During

its continuance, Caroline was feeling at her heart's core what a

dreaming [[Fool|fool]] she was, what an unpractical life she led, how little

fitness there was in her for ordinary intercourse with the ordinary

world. She was feeling how exclusively she had attached herself to the

white cottage in the Hollow, how in the existence of one inmate of that

cottage she had pent all her universe. She was sensible that this would

not do, and that some day she would be forced to make an alteration. It

could not be said that she exactly wished to resemble the ladies before

her, but she wished to become superior to her present [[Self|self]], so as to

feel less scared by their dignity.



The sole means she found of reviving the flagging discourse was by

asking them if they would all stay to tea; and a cruel struggle it cost

her to perform this piece of civility. Mrs. Sykes had begun, "We are

much obliged to you, but----" when in came Fanny once more.



"The gentlemen will stay the evening, ma'am," was the message she

brought from Mr. Helstone.



"What gentlemen have you?" now inquired Mrs. Sykes. Their names were

specified; she and her daughters interchanged glances. The curates were

not to them what they were to Caroline. Mr. Sweeting was quite a

favourite with them; even Mr. Malone rather so, because he was a

clergyman. "Really, since you have company already, I think we will

stay," remarked Mrs. Sykes. "We shall be quite a pleasant little party.

I always like to meet the clergy."



And now Caroline had to usher them upstairs, to help them to unshawl,

smooth their hair, and make themselves smart; to reconduct them to the

drawing-room, to distribute amongst them books of engravings, or odd

things purchased from the Jew-basket. She was obliged to be a purchaser,

though she was but a slack contributor; and if she had possessed plenty

of money, she would rather, when it was brought to the rectory--an awful

incubus!--have purchased the whole stock than contributed a single

pin-cushion.



It ought perhaps to be explained in passing, for the benefit of those

who are not _au fait_ to the mysteries of the "Jew-basket" and

"missionary-basket," that these _meubles_ are willow repositories, of

the capacity of a good-sized family clothes-basket, dedicated to the

purpose of conveying from [[house]] to [[house]] a [[Monster|monster]] collection of

pin-cushions, needle-books, card-racks, workbags, articles of infant

wear, etc., etc., etc., made by the willing or reluctant hands of the

Christian ladies of a parish, and sold perforce to the heathenish

gentlemen thereof, at prices unblushingly exorbitant. The proceeds of

such compulsory sales are applied to the [[Conversion|conversion]] of the Jews, the

seeking up of the ten missing tribes, or to the [[Regeneration|regeneration]] of the

interesting coloured population of the globe. Each lady contributor

takes it in her turn to keep the basket a month, to sew for it, and to

foist off its contents on a shrinking male public. An exciting [[Time|time]] it

is when that turn comes round. Some active-minded woman, with a good

trading spirit, like it, and enjoy exceedingly the fun of making

hard-handed worsted-spinners cash up, to the tune of four or five

hundred per cent. above cost price, for articles quite useless to them;

other feebler souls object to it, and would rather see the prince of

darkness himself at their door any morning than that [[Phantom|phantom]] basket,

brought with "Mrs. Rouse's compliments; and please, ma'am, she says it's

your turn now."



Miss Helstone's duties of hostess performed, more anxiously than

cheerily, she betook herself to the kitchen, to hold a brief

privy-council with Fanny and Eliza about the tea.



"What a lot on 'em!" cried Eliza, who was cook. "And I put off the

baking to-day because I thought there would be bread plenty to fit while

morning. We shall never have enow."



"Are there any tea-cakes?" asked the young mistress.



"Only three and a loaf. I wish these fine folk would stay at [[Home|home]] till

they're asked; and I want to finish trimming my hat" (bonnet she meant).



"Then," suggested Caroline, to whom the importance of the emergency gave

a certain energy, "Fanny must run down to Briarfield and buy some

muffins and crumpets and some biscuits. And don't be [[Cross|cross]], Eliza; we

can't help it now."



"And which tea-things are we to have?"



"Oh, the best, I suppose. I'll get out the silver service." And she ran

upstairs to the plate-closet, and presently brought down teapot,

cream-ewer, and sugar-basin.



"And mun we have th' urn?"



"Yes; and now get it ready as quickly as you can, for the sooner we have

tea over the sooner they will go--at least, I [[Hope|hope]] so. Heigh-ho! I wish

they were gone," she sighed, as she returned to the drawing-room.

"Still," she thought, as she paused at the door ere opening it, "if

Robert would but come even now how bright all would be! How

comparatively easy the task of amusing these people if he were present!

There would be an interest in hearing him talk (though he never says

much in company) and in talking in his presence. There can be no

interest in hearing any of them, or in speaking to them. How they will

gabble when the curates come in, and how weary I shall grow with

listening to them! But I suppose I am a selfish [[Fool|fool]]. These are very

“E c’era anche il dottor Broadbent,” gridò Hannah – “un oratore davvero straordinario!”

Non te lo saresti mai aspettato da lui, perché è un uomo dall'aspetto quasi volgare.



“Ma che uomo gentile,” interruppe Mary.



“E un uomo così buono, così utile,” aggiunse sua madre.



“Solo dall’aspetto sembra un macellaio,” intervenne la bella e orgogliosa Harriet.

La signorina Helstone era consapevole della propria ignoranza e incompetenza. Non avendo mai incontrato il dottore.

“Con la mente altrove, non riusciva a esprimere il proprio parere… Il terzo silenzio calò su di lei.”

Lei, ma desiderava diventare superiore a quella che era ora, per poter.

Sentirsi meno spaventati a causa della loro dignità.



Il solo modo che trovò per ravvivare il dibattito ormai languente fu…

Chiedendo loro se volessero tutti rimanere per il tè… E fu una lotta davvero crudele quella che dovette affrontare.

#Per dimostrare questa cortesia… La signora Sykes aveva iniziato dicendo: “Noi…”

Grazie mille, ma----” proprio in quel momento Fanny tornò di nuovo dentro.



“Gli signori rimarranno a cena, signora,” fu il messaggio che ricevette.

Portato dal signor Helstone.



“Quali signori avete con voi?” chiese la signora Sykes. I loro nomi erano…

# Lo scambio di sguardi  
Lei e le sue figlie si scambiarono occhiate. I curatori…

“Non erano per loro ciò che erano per Caroline… Il signor Sweeting era davvero un…”

#Il preferito di loro; persino il signor Malone lo era, perché…

#Chierico. “Davvero, visto che hai già compagnia, penso che possiamo andare…”

“Rimani,” osservò la signora Sykes. “Sarà davvero una piacevole piccola compagnia.”

Mi piace sempre incontrare il clero.



E ora Caroline doveva accompagnarli al piano di sopra per aiutarli a togliersi i scialli.

#Lisciarsi i capelli e mettersi in ordine; per ricondurli…

#Salotto, per distribuire tra di loro libri di incisioni o oggetti vari

Cose acquistate dal cestino ebreo… Era costretta ad acquistarle.

Nonostante contribuisse in modo scarso… e se avesse posseduto abbastanza…

“Di denaro… preferiva che venisse portato alla canonica… un vero disastro.”

#Incubo: hanno acquistato l’intero lotto senza aver contribuito nemmeno con una singola unità

cuscino a perle.



#For the Benefit of Those...

Chi non è a conoscenza dei misteri del “Cestino Ebraico”…

“Missionary-Basket: questi mobili sono in realtà contenitori fatti di salice…”

# La capienza di un cesto per la biancheria domestica di dimensioni decenti, dedicato a…

Lo scopo era trasportare, da una [[house|>casa]] all’altra, una collezione davvero enorme di [[Monster|mostri]].

“Cuscini da cucito, libri per aghi, portacarte, borse da lavoro… articoli per bambini.”

# Manufatti creati dalle mani, volontarie o meno, di…

#Donne cristiane di una parrocchia… costrette a essere vendute ai pagani

Signori, a prezzi senza vergogna esorbitanti… I proventi derivanti da…

Tali vendite obbligatorie venivano applicate alla [[Conversion|conversione]] degli Ebrei.

La ricerca delle dieci tribù scomparse, o la [[Regeneration|rigenerazione]] di.

Una popolazione colorata e interessante del globo… Ogni signora che contribuisce…

"#Si prende a sua volta il compito di custodire il cesto per un mese, di cucirlo e di…"#

Imponga il proprio contenuto a un pubblico maschile in declino. Un’epoca davvero eccitante, quella.

#Quando arriva quel momento… Una donna con la mente attiva, capace di fare qualcosa di concreto…

# Spirito di intraprendenza: goditi appieno il divertimento di creare e fare

Titolo:  
Gli spinnatori più brutali e spietati incassano somme considerevoli, addirittura quattro o cinque…

Cento percento sopra il prezzo di costo… per articoli del tutto inutili per loro.

Altre anime più deboli si oppongono e preferirebbero vedere il principe…

Nessuna oscurità, in nessuna mattina, sarebbe più terribile di quel cesto fantasma.

Titolo:  
“Portato con i complimenti della signora Rouse; e per favore, signora, dice che…”

Ora è il tuo turno.



#Le mansioni di padrona di casa svolte da Miss Helstone, con maggiore ansia del solito…

Con allegria, si diresse in cucina per occuparsi rapidamente di qualcosa…

Consiglio privato con Fanny ed Eliza riguardo al tè.



“Che quantità…”, esclamò Eliza, che era la cuoca. “E io l’ho rimandato…”

#Cuocendo oggi… perché pensavo ci sarebbe stato abbastanza pane per tutti.

Mattina. Non ne avremo mai abbastanza.



“Ci sono delle tortine al tè?” chiese la giovane padrona di casa.



“Solo tre e un pane. Vorrei che queste brave persone rimanessero a [[Home|>casa]] fino, ”

“Mi stanno chiedendo qualcosa. E voglio finire di sistemare il mio cappello” (intendeva dire il suo cappellino).



“Allora,” suggerì Caroline, consapevole dell’urgenza della situazione.

# Una certa energia… “Fanny deve correre subito a Briarfield e comprare qualcosa”

Muffin, crumpet e alcuni biscotti. E non essere arrabbiata, Eliza; noi.

Ora non posso farci nulla.



“E quali tè dovremo bere?”



“Ah, il meglio, immagino… Tiro fuori la porcellana d’argento.” E corse via.

“Su per le scale, fino all’armadio dove si conservano le tazze da tè… e poco dopo tornò giù con la teiera.”

Cremiera e ciotola per lo zucchero.



“E allora avremo la coppa?”



"Sì; e ora preparatelo il più in fretta possibile, perché prima lo avremo..."

Più presto finiranno la loro tazza di tè, almeno, è quello che [[Hope|>spero]]. Ehi, che peccato.

“Sono andati via,” sospirò lei, rientrando nel salotto.

“Still,” pensò mentre si fermava sulla soglia prima di aprirla, “se…”

# Robert… se solo potesse tornare ora… quanto tutto sarebbe più bello!

Sarebbe stato relativamente facile intrattenere queste persone se lui fosse stato presente.

Ci sarebbe interesse ad ascoltarlo parlare… anche se lui non parla mai.

#In sua presenza… e nel parlare davanti a lui. Non può esserci alcuna possibilità…

# Nessun interesse ad ascoltarli o a parlare con loro… Come faranno…

Ascoltandoli. Ma suppongo di essere un egoista [[Fool|idiota]]. Sono davvero molto.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_07--part_07" data-title="Shirley — Chapter 7 (part 7)" data-chapter="Chapter 07" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/king,motif/silence,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/self,character/sunday"></span>


respectable gentlefolks. I ought, no [[Doubt|doubt]], to be proud of their

countenance. I don't say they are not as good as I am--far from it--but

they are different from me."



She went in.



Yorkshire people in those days took their tea round the table, sitting

[[Well|well]] into it, with their knees duly introduced under the mahogany. It

was essential to have a multitude of plates of bread and butter, varied

in sorts and plentiful in quantity. It was thought proper, too, that on

the centre plate should stand a glass dish of marmalade. Among the

viands was expected to be found a small assortment of cheesecakes and

tarts. If there was also a plate of thin slices of pink ham garnished

with green parsley, so much the better.



Eliza, the rector's cook, fortunately knew her business as provider. She

had been put out of [[Humour|humour]] a little at first, when the invaders came so

unexpectedly in such strength; but it appeared that she regained her

cheerfulness with action, for in due [[Time|time]] the tea was spread forth in

handsome style, and neither ham, tarts, nor marmalade were wanting among

its accompaniments.



The curates, summoned to this bounteous repast, entered joyous; but at

once, on seeing the ladies, of whose presence they had not been

forewarned, they came to a stand in the doorway. Malone headed the

party; he stopped short and fell back, almost capsizing Donne, who was

behind him. Donne, staggering three paces in retreat, sent little

Sweeting into the arms of old Helstone, who brought up the rear. There

was some expostulation, some tittering. Malone was desired to mind what

he was about, and urged to push forward, which at last he did, though

colouring to the top of his peaked forehead a bluish purple. Helstone,

advancing, set the shy curates aside, welcomed all his fair guests,

shook hands and passed a jest with each, and seated himself snugly

between the lovely Harriet and the dashing Hannah. Miss Mary he

requested to move to the seat opposite to him, that he might see her if

he couldn't be near her. Perfectly easy and gallant, in his way, were

his manners always to young ladies, and most popular was he amongst

them; yet at heart he neither respected nor liked the sex, and such of

them as circumstances had brought into intimate relation with him had

ever feared rather than loved him.



The curates were left to shift for themselves. Sweeting, who was the

least embarrassed of the three, took refuge beside Mrs. Sykes, who, he

knew, was almost as fond of him as if he had been her son. Donne, after

making his general bow with a grace all his own, and saying in a high,

pragmatical voice, "How d'ye do, Miss Helstone?" dropped into a seat at

Caroline's elbow, to her unmitigated annoyance, for she had a peculiar

antipathy to Donne, on account of his stultified and immovable

[[Self|self]]-conceit and his incurable narrowness of mind. Malone, grinning most

unmeaningly, inducted himself into the corresponding seat on the other

side. She was thus blessed in a pair of supporters, neither of whom, she

knew, would be of any mortal use, whether for keeping up the

conversation, handing cups, circulating the muffins, or even lifting the

plate from the slop-basin. Little Sweeting, small and boyish as he was,

would have been worth twenty of them.



Malone, though a ceaseless talker when there were only men present, was

usually tongue-tied in the presence of ladies. Three phrases, however,

he had ready cut and dried, which he never failed to produce:--



1stly. "Have you had a walk to-day, Miss Helstone?"



2ndly. "Have you seen your cousin Moore lately?"



3rdly. "Does your class at the [[Sunday]] school keep up its number?"



These three questions being put and responded to, between Caroline and

Malone reigned [[Silence|silence]].



With Donne it was otherwise; he was troublesome, exasperating. He had a

stock of small-talk on hand, at once the most trite and perverse that

can [[Well|well]] be imagined--abuse of the people of Briarfield; of the natives

of Yorkshire generally; complaints of the want of high society; of the

backward state of civilization in these districts; murmurings against

the disrespectful conduct of the lower orders in the north toward their

betters; silly ridicule of the manner of living in these parts--the want

of style, the absence of elegance, as if he, Donne, had been accustomed

to very great doings indeed, an insinuation which his somewhat underbred

manner and aspect failed to bear out. These strictures, he seemed to

think, must raise him in the estimation of Miss Helstone or of any other

lady who heard him; whereas with her, at least, they brought him to a

level below contempt, though sometimes, indeed, they incensed her; for,

a Yorkshire girl herself, she hated to hear Yorkshire abused by such a

pitiful prater; and when wrought up to a certain pitch, she would turn

and say something of which neither the matter nor the manner recommended

her to Mr. Donne's good-will. She would tell him it was no proof of

refinement to be ever scolding others for vulgarity, and no sign of a

good pastor to be eternally censuring his flock. She would ask him what

he had entered the church for, since he complained there were only

cottages to visit, and poor people to preach to--whether he had been

ordained to the ministry merely to wear soft clothing and sit in [[King|king]]'s

houses. These questions were considered by all the curates as, to the

last degree, audacious and impious.



Tea was a long [[Time|time]] in progress; all the guests gabbled as their hostess

had expected they would. Mr. Helstone, being in excellent spirits--when,

indeed, was he ever otherwise in society, attractive female society? it

being only with the one lady of his own family that he maintained a grim

taciturnity--kept up a brilliant flow of easy prattle with his

right-hand and left-hand neighbours, and even with his _vis-à-vis_, Miss
